figures.alt: Color cartoon of giant fat men in top hats labeled with trust names towering over small senators seated at desks, with a sign reading This is a Senate of the monopolists
figures.caption: 'The Bosses of the Senate,' Joseph Keppler, Puck, 1889

options.misconception: Background: the government sided with business — federal troops broke the 1877 strike and an injunction broke Pullman in 1894.
options.text: That the federal government consistently sided with workers against business

options.misconception: Background: trusts and railroads reached every region; Standard Oil was a national company.
options.text: That big business had no influence outside the Northeast
That industrialization concentrated power and wealth in a few hands

options.misconception: Background: unions, the Grange, the Populists, and reformers all challenged business power, even when they lost.
options.text: That ordinary Americans had no way to challenge business power

rationales.A: Background: the government sided with business. Federal troops broke the 1877 strike, and an injunction broke Pullman in 1894.
rationales.B: Background: trusts and railroads reached every region. Standard Oil was a national company, not a Northeastern one.
rationales.C: The giants own the trusts and the Senate while the people's door stays closed. Background: the period's wealth and power piled up with a few owners while workers, farmers, and immigrants shared little of it.
rationales.D: Background: unions, the Grange, the Populists, and reformers all challenged business power — even when they lost the fight.
rationales.general:
Step back from the single cartoon and the whole period comes into focus.
1. Add up the period. Background: railroads, steel, and oil made a few owners rich beyond imagining.
2. Ask who shared the wealth. Background: workers labored long hours for low pay, farmers sank into debt, immigrants crowded into tenements.
3. Name the pattern. Background: power and wealth concentrated in a few hands while most Americans shared little of it.
Remember: the Gilded Age glittered on top and stayed base metal below — the cartoon draws the gap.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Joseph Keppler, Puck, 1889, public domain.
stem: Taken together with the period's other developments, the cartoon best supports which broader conclusion about the Gilded Age?

stimulus.source_note: Joseph Keppler, 'The Bosses of the Senate,' Puck magazine, 1889. Public domain. Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Bosses_of_the_Senate_by_Joseph_Keppler.jpg
stimulus.text: The cartoon shows giant, fat men in top hats towering over the small senators seated at their desks below. Each giant's belly is labeled with a trust: 'Steel Beam Trust,' 'Copper Trust,' 'Standard Oil Trust,' 'Iron Trust,' 'Sugar Trust,' 'Tin Trust,' 'Coal Trust.' A sign on the wall reads: 'This is a Senate of the monopolists, by the monopolists, and for the monopolists!' Above a small side door, a sign reads: 'Peoples' Entrance — CLOSED.'
